mcqs.question: A user with 10,000 notes syncs their notes app, and only one note changed since the last sync. Under full sync versus delta sync, what's the practical difference?
options: Full sync re-downloads all 10,000 notes every time; delta sync downloads only the one changed note, given a server that can answer 'what changed since X'
There is no practical difference — both approaches transfer the same amount of data
Delta sync is always simpler to implement than full sync regardless of backend support
Full sync is only usable for datasets under 100 records total
mcqs.explanation: Full sync's simplicity comes at the cost of re-transferring the entire dataset every time regardless of how much actually changed, while delta sync avoids that but specifically requires backend support for tracking and querying changes since a given point. Delta sync is not inherently simpler to implement — it requires more backend capability — and full sync has no hard record-count ceiling, just a growing cost as data scales.

mcqs.question: Why might a system that needs to correctly detect true concurrent edits (not just conflicting version numbers) use vector clocks instead of plain timestamps?
options: Vector clocks are simpler to implement than timestamps
Timestamps are vulnerable to device clock skew and can't capture causality between edits across multiple devices, which vector clocks are specifically designed to track
Timestamps cannot be stored in most databases
Vector clocks eliminate the need for any conflict resolution strategy entirely
mcqs.explanation: Vector clocks are specifically designed to capture the causal relationship between changes across multiple devices, which plain timestamps can't do reliably given clock drift and the fact that near-simultaneous edits may not be causally related the way their timestamps suggest. Vector clocks are more complex to implement, not simpler, and they don't eliminate the need for a resolution strategy — they just detect concurrency more accurately.

mcqs.question: Two devices edit different fields of the same record while both offline — one changes a note's title, the other changes its body. Which conflict resolution strategy correctly preserves both edits?
options: Last-write-wins, since the later edit should always take precedence
Field-level merge, which tracks changes at field granularity and can combine both edits instead of discarding one
Manual resolution is the only strategy capable of handling this case
This scenario cannot be resolved automatically under any strategy
mcqs.explanation: Field-level merge is specifically designed for exactly this case — different fields changed independently can both be kept, since the conflict is only apparent at the whole-record level, not the field level. LWW would discard one edit wholesale even though the edits don't actually conflict, and manual resolution isn't the only option — it's a heavier fallback for cases automatic merging can't safely handle.

mcqs.question: What does a CRDT-based counter track differently from a plain shared integer that two devices might both try to increment?
options: It tracks increments per-device separately and sums them on merge, so concurrent increments from different devices are never lost to a race
It stores the same single integer but locks it during any update from any device
It requires a server to serialize every increment before any device can apply it locally
It rounds concurrent increments down to avoid double-counting
mcqs.explanation: A CRDT counter's defining trick is tracking each source's contributions separately and summing them, which makes the merge mathematically well-defined regardless of arrival order — that's what 'conflict-free' means here. It doesn't rely on locking, doesn't require server-side serialization to stay correct offline, and doesn't need to round anything down since nothing is actually racing on shared mutable state.

mcqs.question: A shared document app uses last-write-wins for the document body. Two users edit the same paragraph while both offline, then both sync. What happens to the user whose edit synced first?
options: Their edit is merged automatically with the other user's edit
The app detects the conflict and prompts both users to choose
Their edit is silently discarded and replaced by the later-syncing edit, with no indication anything was lost
Both edits are kept as separate versions the user can restore later
mcqs.explanation: LWW's whole design resolves the conflict by discarding the losing edit outright with no merge, no prompt, and typically no visible trace — which is exactly why it's the wrong strategy for data where a silently lost edit is a real, user-visible problem. Field-level merge, manual resolution, or version history would each behave differently, but plain LWW behaves exactly as described here.

mcqs.question: A sync operation with no idempotency key succeeds on the server, but the client never receives the confirmation and retries the same push. What's the likely outcome?
options: The server automatically recognizes and ignores the duplicate with no extra mechanism needed
The retry has no effect, since the server already has the correct final state
The client detects the missing confirmation and cancels the retry automatically
The operation is applied a second time, since the server has no way to distinguish the retry from a genuinely new request
mcqs.explanation: Without an idempotency key, the server can't tell a legitimate retry apart from a brand-new request, so the operation gets applied twice — an increment runs twice, a create duplicates a record. This is the standard at-least-once delivery problem, and none of it resolves automatically without the client and server explicitly coordinating on a stable idempotency key.
